pending_items.title: Anti-Zionist Jews and Holocaust survivors accuse UK government of 'dismissive treatment'
pending_items.content:
Anti-Zionist Jewish activists and Holocaust survivors say they have been “ignored” by the UK government, saying that their "dismissive treatment" in contrast to the treatment of pro- Israel groups is "antisemitic".

Jewish Voice for Labour, and Holocaust survivors and descendants - Stephen Kapos, Agnes Kory and Chris Romberg - said that they had experienced months of “unsatisfactory correspondence” with government ministers.

A request for a meeting to discuss their concerns about the government’s treatment of pro- Palestine Jews had gone unanswered.

An open letter - which was addressed to Sarah Jones, minister for policing, and Florence Eshalomi, minister for communities and faith - remains unacknowledged a month on.

By contrast, it pointed to numerous meetings “at many levels of government, from the prime minister down, with pro-Israel organisations and individuals”.

It said that the disparity in this treatment is, in itself, antisemitic.

“Ignoring the many Jews who do not conform with the established narrative of universal support for Israel and Zionism is a position that is itself antisemitic, as it generalises about Jews, reduces them to stereotypes, denies them individuality and agency, and may even endanger their safety, by suggesting that they all support Israel's genocidal actions in Palestine,” the group said.

They said that the letter follows six months of “unsatisfactory correspondence”, which began in May.

That was when some 40 descendants of Holocaust survivors wrote to then Prime Minister Keir Starmer, the Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood and Metropolitan Police Commissioner Mark Rowley refuting allegations that pro-Palestine protests presented a threat to the Jewish community.

“Six weeks later, a junior minister for policing sent us a really anodyne letter just stating government policy,” Romberg told Middle East Eye.

“We had made the point that the only hostility that we actually face on these protests comes from Zionist counter-protesters,’ he said.

“And the letter we got back said, 'Oh, very sorry that you've had this aggression,' but seemed to imply no recognition at all that it was from the counter-protesters."

The group then wrote to incoming Prime Minister Andy Burnham and said that, since then, they have received three letters from the two ministers which they described as being “dismissive in tone” and containing “generalised statements of government policy, much of it irrelevant to the issues we raised”.

They said that the ministers were slow to respond, with one taking two months to reply.

A government spokesperson told MEE in response to a request for comment that they "regularly engage with a wide range of organisations to discuss their concerns and remain committed to working with our Jewish communities".

Last month, the group received a letter from Jones saying that “this government recognises the diversity of our Jewish communities” and expressing commitment to “meaningful engagement with a range of different voices and perspectives”.

“We thought, good, that's healthy. Let's follow that up,” Romberg, a retired British Army colonel, said. “We're not getting anywhere with these letters. We had been waiting six months with all this, so we asked if we could have a meeting in two weeks.”

“It's now been four weeks, and we haven’t even had an acknowledgement,” Romberg said.

The statement noted the “complete contrast” in the government’s attitude to pro-Israel groups, saying that they were not aware of either Burnham or his predecessor holding a single meeting with Jewish pro-Palestine or anti-Zionist organisations.

“The approach the government is taking is actually an approach that is itself in danger of being antisemitic,” Romberg told MEE.

'The approach the government is taking is actually an approach that is itself in danger of being antisemitic'

- Chris Romberg, Holocaust survivor descendant

“They seem to want to ignore Jewish groups that do not fit in with their stereotypical view of what Jews should be. That Jews should support Israel. Jews should be pro-Zionist. And when there are groups that do not fit into that narrative, then they just want to ignore them and won't engage with them.”

MEE is aware of numerous meetings in the last 12 months between government ministers and the Board of Deputies of British Jews, the Jewish Leadership Council - both of whom intervened in the appeal of the government's ban on direct action group Palestine Action - and the Community Security Trust.

In the months before the proscription of Palestine Action, Met chief Rowley met with the Jewish Board of Deputies on 6 November 2024 to discuss a series of actions by the group.

A government spokesperson said that: "As the Court of Appeal found, Palestine Action is not a civil disobedience protest group but one that carried out acts of terrorism, celebrated those who took part in them and promoted the use of violence."

Declassified has revealed that a number of meetings between ministers and pro-Israel lobbyists were unminuted, including an off-the-record meeting between then Foreign Minister David Lammy and pro-Israeli businessman Trevor Chinn in February 2025.

Another meeting between Middle East Minister Hamish Falconer and Chinn a month later was also not recorded in transparency data.

Romberg said he had “very low expectations” that things would shift under Burnham’s government, despite the prime minister’s admission that his party “got it wrong on Gaza” and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s imposition of sanctions on settlements.

“I feel this is deflectionary. This is a recognition of electoral pressures. Words are easy,” Romberg said.

“There’s been a lot of clucking, but there haven't actually been any eggs laid,” he added.

pending_items.title: ‘Symbolic’: Why did UK sanction Yemen’s Houthis amid attacks on Saudi?
pending_items.content:
London, United Kingdom – The United Kingdom has slapped sanctions on Yemen’s Houthis and four of their senior leaders after accusing the Iran-backed group of renewed “aggression” inside Yemen and attacks targeting civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.

The Houthis have escalated attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting the financial district in Riyadh this week, as they engage in a civil war with Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

Fighting has escalated since July as a 2022 United Nations-brokered ceasefire collapsed. Since then, the Houthis have captured the Red Sea port of Mocha and the island of Mayyun, extending control over the Red Sea in a setback to the Saudi-backed government.

The war erupted after the Houthis captured the capital, Sanaa, in late 2014, forcing President Abd Rabbu Mansour Hadi to flee. Saudi Arabia intervened in support of the Hadi government as it saw the Iran-backed group’s rise in neighbouring Yemen as a security threat.

The UK government announced its sanctions on Tuesday, accusing the Houthis of undermining peace and security in Yemen and the region. It froze assets and placed travel bans on the group and its leaders, including Interior Minister Abdulkarim Amir al-Din Hussein al-Houthi and Security and Intelligence chief Abdul Hakim Hashem Ali al-Khaiwani.

Chief prosecutor Sarim al-Din Mufadal, who has been accused of perpetrating “sexual violence, including rape and torture”, also faces an asset freeze and travel ban.

“The Houthis’ renewed aggression targeting our partners and innocent civilians is unacceptable, and they must be held to account,” said UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who linked the sanctions to attacks on shipping in the Bab al-Mandeb strait in the Red Sea, one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world.

“Today’s measures send a clear message to the Houthis – we will always act in support of British values and interests,” he said in a statement.

The British move comes nearly a month after it decided to deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia, a close ally going back decades that has increasingly come under missile and drone attacks in recent weeks.

Britain also sent Tornado fighters to Saudi Arabia in the wake of the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait in 1990, according to the Royal Air Force Museum.

The Houthis have also targeted oil installations and a major pipeline that helped Saudi Arabia export its oil while Iran essentially blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint. Tehran said it has blocked the vital waterway, through which most of the Gulf oil and natural gas passes, in response to the US-Israel war on Iran.

The UK has naval and logistics bases in the neighbouring Gulf nations of Bahrain and Oman. In May, it agreed a free trade deal with the six Gulf Cooperation Council states.

Thomas Juneau, an associate fellow with Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme, said the sanctions were imposed during a diplomatic push by Riyadh.

“Saudi Arabia has been asking other countries to list the Houthis as a terrorist entity, to turn the screw on the Houthis and to help in its campaign against the group,” he told Al Jazeera.

The sanctions, Ahmed Nagi from the International Crisis Group (ICG) said, are “intended to send a political message about where the UK stands on the current escalation and the Houthi actions”.

In January 2024, the UK and the United States jointly sanctioned four Houthi figures, including the group’s defence minister and naval commander, over attacks on Red Sea shipping, and a month later, a second package targeted the Quds Force, the overseas unit of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The same month, the UK joined the US in carrying out air strikes on Houthi positions over attacks on ships in the Red Sea, which had disrupted maritime trade. The Houthis had imposed a ban on ships linked to Israel from passing through the waterway in response to Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

The Houthis are already under a UN arms embargo, and London is now “going further”, Nagi, who is a senior Yemen analyst at the ICG, said.

This month, the UN Security Council renewed its Yemen sanctions regime until November 2027 through a UK-led resolution.

Raiman al-Hamdani, a Yemeni researcher and analyst, said the UK, as the Security Council’s lead on Yemen, had helped shape that regime and “this latest step continues a longstanding policy rather than breaking from it.”

But Nagi called the UK move “largely symbolic”.

“The four Houthi leaders targeted by the sanctions are unlikely to travel to the UK or hold assets there, so the practical impact will probably be limited.”

Al-Hamdani said the group’s income comes “largely from the black market, smuggling, taxation of local businesses and control of ports and customs, none of which a UK asset freeze touches”.

“The missile and drone programme hasn’t slowed despite years of UN, US, EU and UK listings,” he added.

Juneau from Chatham House agreed the sanctions would not change Houthi behaviour soon but said that while sanctions by individual countries other than the US have little effect alone, they can matter collectively, which is why Saudi Arabia is pressing as many countries as possible to act.

He also pointed to the Houthis’ growing influence in the Red Sea, which has concerned Saudi Arabia as well as its Western allies.

The British foreign secretary on Tuesday pointed out how Houthi actions in the Red Sea were “driving up the cost of living for the British people” and “undermining the stability of the Middle East”.

Analysts pointed out that the UK government statement is silent on the other parties to the war – the Yemeni government forces and Saudi Arabia – even as it said the Houthis’ “reckless aggression is responsible for this conflict”.

Nagi said the omission reflected how London sees the war.

“From London’s perspective, the Houthis are the ones attacking Saudi Arabia and escalating the conflict, rather than the other way around,” he said.

Juneau was blunter. “Sanctions are always political. You sanction your opponents. You don’t sanction your partners or friends,” he said.

Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch, expressed concerns that the sanctions would impact aid organisations engaged in humanitarian work in Houthi-held areas.

“As Yemen relies heavily on imports, curbs affecting commercial goods could also push up food prices,” she told Al Jazeera.

“The sanctions really can have quite devastating impacts for the populations living in territories under Houthi control, even if that’s not what the UK intends by the sanctions,” she warned.

This is the case even though the UK’s sanctions already include a humanitarian exception covering aid and other activities that meet basic human needs, she said.

Moreover, the UK has not proscribed the Houthis under “antiterrorism” laws despite its other Western allies – the US, Canada and Australia – designating the Iran-backed group as a “terrorist” organisation.

Juneau called the aid agencies’ fear that proscription could hamper humanitarian deliveries “a valid concern” although some people argued the Houthis’ diversion of aid has already made such work extremely difficult.

The Houthis have repeatedly denied that they have diverted humanitarian aid.

Al-Hamdani said sanctions have not forced the Houthis to change their tactics. They do not “appear to respond to human rights criticism or listings”, he said, adding that the group “tends to treat detainees and abuses as bargaining chips to strengthen its negotiating position and demands”.

Rather, he said, sanctions “risk deepening polarisation and closing off the political settlement the war needs”.

pending_items.title: James ‘Fergie’ Chambers: US trying to cast ‘antiwar ideas as extremist’
pending_items.content:
Madrid, Spain – James “Fergie” Chambers, a pro-Palestine philanthropist who is the subject of an ongoing extradition request by the United States government, said he believed the US is targeting supporters of the people of Gaza worldwide.

The US government’s case centres on Chambers’s alleged laundering of $7.5m, which he is said to have wired several years ago from a US bank account to Tunisia, where he lived at the time, allegedly using the cash to support Hamas.

He is not charged with any “terrorism” offences and denies any wrongdoing.

Chambers, a self-proclaimed Marxist-Leninist and the heir to the Cox Enterprises media fortune, believes supporters of the Palestinian cause are being targeted around the globe.

“I think that when the neocolonial system starts to break apart economically, militarily, which I believe is happening, it becomes desperate. And when it becomes desperate, it becomes more violent and more violent,” he told Al Jazeera.

“And all these things sort of converge around the occupation of Palestine because we understand the occupation of Palestine as basically nothing more than an expression of US military and business interest. So that is the focal point of repression.”

He added: “In relation to the Palestinian cause and other causes, I think there is a kind of effort certainly in the US to designate [expressing] antiwar ideas as extremist and terrorist.”

Chambers, who was released from prison in Madrid on bail last week after serving four months on remand, said he was being targeted by the US because of his support for the Palestinian cause.

“I’m not even accused of sending money anywhere illegal. I’m accused of wanting to, which is sort of a crazy distinction to me. They haven’t accused me of sending money to Hamas, no. They’ve accused me of wanting to send money to Hamas,” he said.

A keen football fan, he said he transferred the money to Club Africain, a Tunisian football team, which he sponsors.

He said he had met someone from the Iranian embassy in Tunisia at an international book fair in 2023.

“[They] tied in a narrative which says that … I allegedly visited the Iranian diplomats, which is not true. I met someone from the Iranian embassy at an international book fair, who told me that US citizens are allowed to have tourist visas. I never met an official at the embassy. I never went into the offices at the embassy.”

The 41-year-old said a forensic accountant had presented Club Africain’s accounts to the Madrid court.

As part of a deal in which his family cut ties with him at the time, he sold stock back to his family worth about $250m in mid-2023.

“I’m assuming the implication is that I would have met with these people and then transferred money to Tunisia to a football club with the intention of then laundering it to Hamas.”

The US Department of Justice said it did not want to comment when contacted by Al Jazeera.

Chambers said he was “very publicly” affiliated with the club, which won the Tunisian championship this year, and he made a four-year sponsorship deal.

“They had millions of euros worth of debt, which is why they contacted me to get involved. And the money was used to pay off debts, to revamp the team facilities, training facilities, youth programmes, pay overdue salaries. And then in return I had some involvement in management,” he said.

Chambers also said Tunisia was a “closed economy”.

“When you move money into Tunisia, you’re not allowed to move it out,” he said, adding that one of his “most constant emotions in all of this is just downright confusion”.

Chambers, who has given financial aid to 100 projects in 20 countries, including some in Palestine, said he was always careful to obey the law.

“There is no smoking gun. There’s no unloaded gun. There’s nowhere that I said I wanted to support any illegal groups,” he said.

Chambers said he was a target for supporting the Palestinian cause.

“I think the combination of an overall effort by the US authorities to criminalise basically the Palestinian cause in any capacity … this is a part of that,” he said. “You know the fact that I happen to have a lot of resources. And I speak out unapologetically and freely about my positions on US imperialism. These things just combined to make me a target and an example.”

The father-of-four, who has been reunited with his family after being released on bail, is awaiting the court’s decision. His case has also drawn attention to concerns about the implications of the US extradition request.

During his time in jail, he said he received letters of support from many strangers as well as political parties from all sides.

“Even within the prison staff, there was a kind of consensus that people saw me as being somebody who shouldn’t be there,” he said.

However, he said he faces an uncertain future.

“I still don’t know … whether I am going to face decades of my life in a federal penitentiary in the US,” he said.

The High Court said it had decided to release Chambers after US authorities acknowledged what they described as substantial and unintentional errors in the Spanish translation of an FBI agent’s sworn statement, submitted in support of the extradition request. The proceedings have been the subject of further reporting on the extradition case in Spain.

Chambers was arrested on an Interpol Red Notice in Ibiza in July, but has since applied for asylum in Spain.

He cannot be extradited until the asylum claim is resolved, and if it is successful, he cannot be extradited from Spain to the US at all.

pending_items.title: Israeli army used 'trembling' 16-year-old boy as human shield in Gaza, soldier testimonies reveal
pending_items.content:
Israeli soldiers have described the widespread use of Palestinians as human shields in the Gaza Strip, including one boy who was just 16 years old.

Soldiers described sending unarmed civilians ahead of troops to search for fighters and explosives in a practice they called the "Mosquito Protocol".

The investigation, broadcast by public channel Kan on Wednesday, featured testimonies from several officers and combatants.

They described how Palestinian civilians, arrested at checkpoints and elsewhere, were handcuffed and forced to search buildings and tunnels before Israeli troops entered.

“The need to use the ‘shawish’ was to make the explosive device detonate on him rather than, God forbid, on a soldier,” one officer said, referring to Palestinian prisoners.

“I will always prefer Israeli army soldiers over citizens of an enemy state,” he added.

All the officers interviewed appeared with their faces blurred and were identified by pseudonyms.

The programme had already sparked outrage among ministers and lawmakers before its broadcast, with some calling for it to be censored or cancelled.

Defence Minister Israel Katz said the report could “damage the good name of soldiers and commanders, and even expose them to legal risks in the international arena”. He also claimed it would reveal the army's operational methods.

Avigdor Lieberman, leader of the Yisrael Beytenu party, warned that the programme would be used “to spread blood libels against IDF (Israeli army) soldiers”.

An infantry brigade combatant, identified by the pseudonym Ron, said he first learnt about the practice after overhearing a conversation in which a company commander told another officer: “Bring me two Yatomim” - a Hebrew word meaning "orphans" which they used to refer to human shields.

“The following day, the interrogator accompanying my battalion came over and brought me these two young men. He told me: ‘These are two people we arrested along the axis. Use them to enter buildings. Try not to beat them too much,’” Ron said.

'One of them was a 16-year-old boy who was trembling. Both were handcuffed, with their hands behind their backs'

A platoon commander later explained that the men were to be used as human shields, sent ahead of troops to "open doors" and enter positions before them.

“That way, if there was an explosive device, it would explode on them rather than on us,” Ron said.

“One of them was a 16-year-old boy who was trembling. Both were handcuffed, with their hands behind their backs,” he recalled.

“Every time before they entered a position, we removed the plastic covering over their eyes, but we did not remove their restraints.”

In June 2025, the United Nations said it had verified the use of 27 Palestinian boys as human shields by Israeli armed forces during operations in the Gaza Strip (22) and the occupied West Bank (five).

Ron described the experience as “horrific” because soldiers had to accompany the handcuffed prisoners to the bathroom.

“I'm sure the experience was even more terrifying for them,” he added.

Another officer said Palestinians were selected after their faces were scanned by a device. If it showed green, indicating that the person was not affiliated with an armed group in Gaza, they could be selected for the practice.

Those chosen were usually young men aged between 20 and 30.

Adam, another officer, said that on one occasion, commanders told troops they would not have a canine unit but would instead be provided with Palestinian human shields.
